description: We are a team of two students with diverse and complementary skills. Fathima is a Cybersecurity Engineering student with a strong background in web development, programming, and design. Avishanth is an Environmental Health and Safety student interested in sustainability, health, and safety. Together, we combine technical expertise, creativity, and environmental awareness to approach challenges from different perspectives and develop innovative solutions.
summary:
We developed EmberWatch, an interactive web app that uses NASA satellite observations to show where fires are being detected and how current burning activity compares with historical patterns. The project addresses a challenge in comparing more than two decades of fire observations. MODIS and VIIRS detect fires at different resolutions, so a jump in raw hotspot counts can reflect a change in instruments. EmberWatch groups detections into a common grid, counts each active cell once per day, and uses years when both instruments operated to improve comparability.

Users can explore recent detections on a global map, compare regional fire seasons, and see when activity is unusually high for the time of year. This context helps communities, researchers, and preparedness teams interpret satellite observations and decide where closer monitoring may be warranted.
details:
EmberWatch combines active-fire detections from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) with weather and air-quality data accessed through Open-Meteo. The app displays recent hotspots on an interactive map and organises historical activity into a calendar. Its anomaly view compares the latest 30 days with the same calendar window in past years, so users can distinguish a typical seasonal peak from unusually high activity.

One of our creative features, Fire Memory, finds past episodes in the same region with similar conditions and shows how burning activity unfolded over the following 30 days. A separate what-if tool lets users explore how changing temperature, rainfall, humidity, or wind affects the model’s outlook. Users can bring these observations into a printable briefing for preparedness discussions. We designed the app to make satellite data easier to interpret and share, especially when teams need to explain why current conditions deserve attention.

We built the data pipeline and FastAPI backend in Python, using DuckDB and Parquet to process and query satellite records. We built the interface with React and TypeScript, using MapLibre GL JS for the map and Recharts for charts.

We considered differences in sensor resolution, duplicate detections from overlapping satellite passes, gaps in coverage, and how to communicate uncertainty. Users can compare the harmonised calendar with each sensor’s record and inspect data coverage. The app also shows forecast ranges, while forecast skill metrics are pending until sufficient verified historical data is available for evaluation.
